lessons.prologue: Before a single Roman road was built across Britain, dozens of proud Iron Age tribes farmed green valleys, crowned hilltops with giant earth ramparts, and twisted pure gold into gleaming neck rings. Step inside a smoky thatched roundhouse to discover how Celtic Britons really lived!
lessons.blurb: Before a single Roman road was built across Britain, dozens of proud Iron Age tribes farmed green valleys, crowned hilltops with giant earth ramparts, and twisted pure gold into gleaming neck rings. Step inside a smoky thatched roundhouse to discover how Celtic Britons really lived!

teacher_notes.primer: This opening enquiry introduces Years 3–4 pupils to Iron Age Celtic Britain (c. 500 BC – AD 43) before the Roman conquest. Pupils overturn the common misconception that pre-Roman Britons were "primitive cavemen" by exploring tribal kingdoms (Iceni, Catuvellauni, Brigantes), giant earthwork hillforts like Maiden Castle, clever chimney-free roundhouse engineering, Druid oral traditions, dazzling gold torcs and bronze shields, and cross-Channel trade alongside Julius Caesar's brief landings in 55 BC and 54 BC.

items.question: On a history timeline, what do the letters "BC" after a date stand for?
items.answer: Before Christ (years counted backwards before AD 1)
items.explanation: In BC dates, bigger numbers happened longer ago — so 500 BC came centuries before 55 BC!

items.question: On a history timeline, which happened earlier: 500 BC or AD 43?
items.explanation: All BC ("Before Christ") years happened before AD ("Anno Domini") years began.

items.question: Great Britain is surrounded completely by sea. What geographical word describes land surrounded by water?
items.explanation: Because Great Britain is an island, ancient visitors and armies had to cross the sea in wooden ships.

items.question: Which narrow stretch of sea separates southern England from France and mainland Europe?
items.explanation: On a clear day, white chalk cliffs can be seen across the narrowest part of the English Channel.

items.question: In which sunny southern European country is the ancient city of Rome located?
items.explanation: Rome began as a city in Italy shaped like a boot stretching into the warm Mediterranean Sea.

items.question: Why do historians call the period before the Romans arrived in Britain the "Iron Age"?
items.answer: Because people learned to heat and hammer iron to make strong tools and weapons
items.explanation: Iron ploughs, axes, and swords were stronger and sharper than earlier Stone Age or Bronze Age tools.

items.question: Before cars, trains, or paved roads existed, how did people carry heavy goods between Britain and Europe?
items.answer: By wooden sailing and rowing boats across rivers and seas
items.explanation: Water travel by river and sea was much faster for heavy cargo than dragging carts through muddy forests.

items.question: Which country lies directly across the English Channel to the south-east of England (called "Gaul" in ancient times)?
items.explanation: Ancient Romans called the lands of modern France and Belgium "Gaul".

items.question: If an ancient community never wrote down books or letters, how do archaeologists find out how they lived?
items.answer: By digging up artefacts, coins, bones, and building remains left in the ground
items.explanation: Objects left behind in soil and rivers give historians physical clues about everyday life long ago.

items.question: What everyday foods can farming families make when they grow fields of wheat and keep cows and sheep?
items.answer: Bread or porridge from wheat flour, plus milk, cheese, meat, and warm wool
items.explanation: Farming allowed ancient families to settle in permanent villages and store grain for winter.

vocab.definition: A circular Iron Age family home with woven clay walls, a central fire, and a tall cone-shaped thatched roof with no chimney.
A settlement built high on a hilltop and ringed with steep earth banks (ramparts), deep ditches, and wooden fences for protection.
Woven strips of bendy hazel wood (wattle) plastered with a sticky mixture of clay, mud, animal dung, and straw (daub) to make warm walls.
A heavy, twisted neck ring made of gold, silver, or bronze worn by wealthy Celtic rulers and warriors to show high status.
Powerful Celtic priests, judges, and teachers who memorised thousands of sacred laws and poems instead of writing books.

narrative_blocks.title: Tribes, Warriors & Giant Earth Hillforts
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] Long before Roman soldiers marched into Britain, the island was home to **Iron Age Celts**. Britain was not one united country with a single ruler. Instead, dozens of proud **tribes** ruled their own lands, including the **Iceni** in the east, the **Catuvellauni** in the south, and the **Brigantes** in the north.

[1.2] Rival tribes sometimes raided neighbours for cattle, so families built giant **hillforts** like **Maiden Castle** in Dorset, ringed with steep earth **ramparts** and wooden fences. When the Roman general **Julius Caesar** landed in **55 BC** and **54 BC**, fierce Celtic warriors in rattling chariots fought bravely before he sailed back to Gaul.

narrative_blocks.title: Inside a Smoky Thatched Roundhouse
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.3] Most Celtic families were hardworking farmers who lived inside circular homes called **roundhouses**. Builders wove hazel branches into **wattle-and-daub** walls plastered with sticky clay, mud, and straw. Overhead rose a tall cone-shaped **thatched roof** of reeds or straw, cleverly built with **no chimney** so howling winds could not blow sparks inside.

[1.4] Smoke from the glowing central **hearth fire** drifted slowly through the thatch, curing meat hung in the rafters and driving away biting insects. Inside the warm, dim room, parents wove brightly patterned woollen cloaks on tall wooden **looms**, while children turned heavy stone **quern stones** to grind wheat into flour.

narrative_blocks.title: Master Craftworkers, Druids & Sea Traders
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.5] Far from being uncivilised, the Celts were dazzling metalworkers and wise storytellers. Smiths twisted ropes of pure gold into heavy neck rings called **torcs**, and decorated **bronze shields** with swirling red glass before offering them to water gods in sacred rivers. Religious leaders called **Druids** never wrote books, instead memorising thousands of laws, poems, and prayers.

[1.6] Celtic Britons were also busy international **sea traders**. Ships crossed the **English Channel** carrying **Cornish tin**, iron, cattle hides, hunting dogs, and golden **wheat** to mainland Europe. Wealthy tribal rulers even minted shiny **gold stater coins**, bringing news of Britain's rich treasures straight to greedy ears in **Rome**.

tasks.model_answer: Iron Age builders cleverly gave their thatched roundhouses no chimney hole because an open hole at the top would act like a wind tunnel, sucking glowing sparks from the central hearth fire straight into the dry straw roof! As it drifted upwards, the smoke cured meat hanging in the rafters so food lasted all winter and drove away biting insects from the family below.

tasks.question: Big Question: Who were the Iron Age Celts, and why is it unfair to call Britain "backward" before the Romans arrived?
tasks.starter: Before the Roman legions arrived in AD 43, the Iron Age Celts were far from backward because...

tasks.model_answer: Before the Roman legions arrived in AD 43, the Iron Age Celts were far from backward because they were clever builders, skilled farmers, master smiths, and international sea traders. Proud tribes such as the Iceni, Catuvellauni, and Brigantes engineered giant earth hillforts like Maiden Castle and cosy wattle-and-daub roundhouses. Their smiths twisted pure gold into gleaming torcs, while ships traded Cornish tin, wheat, and gold stater coins across the English Channel. People only underestimated them later because Druids memorised laws by heart rather than writing books, leaving Romans to write the history!

lessons.prologue: In AD 43, hundreds of Roman warships appeared through the sea mist off the coast of Kent carrying 40,000 armored soldiers — followed weeks later by Emperor Claudius and trumpeting war elephants! Why did Claudius want Britain so badly, and what made the Roman army so tough to beat?
lessons.blurb: In AD 43, hundreds of Roman warships appeared through the sea mist off the coast of Kent carrying 40,000 armored soldiers — followed weeks later by Emperor Claudius and trumpeting war elephants! Why did Claudius want Britain so badly, and what made the Roman army so tough to beat?

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry investigates the causes and events of the Roman invasion of AD 43. Pupils distinguish between Emperor Claudius's personal motive (winning military glory to silence Roman senators who mocked his limp and stutter) and Rome's economic motives (silver, Cornish tin, lead, iron, wheat, and taxes). They then examine the professional Roman legionary's equipment and teamwork (caligae, lorica segmentata, scutum, testudo, bending pilum, and gladius) before following General Aulus Plautius's landing at Richborough, the Battle of the Medway against Caratacus, and Claudius's dramatic entry into Camulodunum (Colchester) with war elephants.

objectives.objective: Explain both the personal and economic reasons why Emperor Claudius invaded Britain in AD 43.
objectives.primer: Connect Claudius's need to prove himself to Roman senators with Britain's silver, tin, lead, iron, wheat, and taxes.
objectives.question: Did Claudius invade Britain mainly for Britain's metals and wheat, or to prove himself as emperor?

objectives.objective: Analyse how Roman legionary training, armour, weapons, and the testudo formation worked together.

objectives.question: Why was a bending javelin (pilum) and a locked tortoise shield wall so effective against Celtic warriors?

objectives.objective: Trace the key events of the AD 43 invasion from Richborough and the River Medway to Camulodunum.
objectives.primer: Follow Aulus Plautius's 40,000 troops, Caratacus's resistance, and Claudius's war elephants at Colchester.
objectives.question: Why did General Aulus Plautius wait by the Thames so Claudius could capture Camulodunum himself?

source_context.Source A: Before becoming emperor in AD 41, Claudius had been mocked by his own family and Roman senators because of his limp and stammer. Sculptors carved noble marble statues across the Empire to present him as a strong, wise, victorious ruler. **Hinge Question:** Why did Emperor Claudius need a famous victory in faraway Britain even more than earlier Roman rulers?
source_context.Source B: Instead of one stiff, heavy breastplate, Roman blacksmiths riveted curved strips of iron onto internal leather straps. This allowed a legionary to breathe, bend, build forts, and march 20 miles a day while turning aside sharp sword slashes. **Hinge Question:** Why was overlapping strip armour much more practical for marching Roman legionaries than a single solid piece of metal?
source_context.Source C: Celtic warriors were brave fighters who swung long iron swords overhead, needing room around them. Roman legionaries fought shoulder-to-shoulder as one tight machine behind locked scutum shields, thrusting forward with short gladius swords. **Hinge Question:** Even though Celtic warriors were tall, fearless fighters, why did Roman equipment and teamwork usually win pitched battles?
source_context.Source D: Richborough guarded the Kent coast where General Aulus Plautius landed his 40,000 troops in AD 43. Notice in Cassius Dio's history that Roman soldiers were frightened at first to sail "outside the limits of the known world", before Claudius arrived with elephants! **Hinge Question:** Why did General Aulus Plautius pause near the River Thames and wait for Emperor Claudius to arrive in person before capturing Camulodunum?

items.question: How was Iron Age Britain organised before the Romans invaded — as one single kingdom or many separate tribes?
items.answer: Many separate tribes (such as the Iceni, Catuvellauni, and Brigantes)
items.explanation: Dozens of proud Celtic tribes ruled their own territories rather than obeying one ruler of all Britain.

items.question: Name the giant Iron Age hillfort in Dorset ringed with steep earth ramparts.
items.explanation: Maiden Castle in Dorset protected families, cattle, and grain behind huge chalk and earth ramparts.

items.question: In which two BC years did the Roman general Julius Caesar briefly land in Britain before sailing back to Gaul?
items.explanation: Julius Caesar crossed the Channel in 55 BC and 54 BC, nearly ninety-seven years before Claudius's invasion.

items.question: What circular Iron Age homes had wattle-and-daub walls and a steep cone thatched roof?
items.explanation: Celtic farming families lived, wove cloth, and cooked around a central hearth fire inside roundhouses.

items.question: Why did Iron Age builders leave NO chimney hole at the top of a thatched roundhouse roof?
items.answer: To stop wind blowing sparks into the dry thatch, while rising smoke cured meat and kept insects out
items.explanation: Smoke seeped safely through the straw roof instead of rushing up a draughty chimney.

items.question: What heavy hand-turned stones did Celtic children use to grind wheat into flour?
items.explanation: Turning rotary quern stones ground grain into fresh flour beside the hearth fire.

items.question: What heavy twisted gold neck rings did wealthy Celtic leaders wear to show their high status?
items.explanation: Master smiths twisted ropes of pure gold into gleaming neck rings such as the Snettisham Great Torc.

items.question: Who were the wise Celtic priests and judges who memorised thousands of laws and prayers instead of writing books?
items.explanation: Druids passed down Celtic laws, poems, and religious knowledge entirely by memory.

current_items.question: Which Roman Emperor ordered the massive invasion of Britain in AD 43?
current_items.explanation: Emperor Claudius wanted military glory to impress doubting Roman senators as well as Britain's rich metals and wheat.

current_items.question: Name three valuable underground metals Rome wanted from British mines.
current_items.answer: Silver, Cornish tin, lead, and iron
current_items.explanation: Rome used silver for coins, lead for water pipes, and tin and iron for bronze and weapons.

current_items.question: What was the Roman "testudo" ("tortoise") formation?
current_items.answer: Soldiers locking curved scutum shields in front and overhead like a tortoise shell against arrows
current_items.explanation: Locking rectangular scutum shields protected advancing legionaries from spears, stones, and arrows.

current_items.question: Why was a Roman legionary's throwing javelin (pilum) designed to bend when it hit an enemy shield?
current_items.answer: So enemies could not pull it out and throw it back, and it weighed down their shield
current_items.explanation: Once the soft iron neck of a pilum bent on impact, the enemy warrior had to drop his tangled shield.

current_items.question: Roughly how many Roman troops landed with General Aulus Plautius at Richborough in Kent in AD 43, and what animals did Claudius bring to Colchester?
current_items.answer: Around 40,000 soldiers — followed by Claudius bringing war elephants!
current_items.explanation: Four legions plus auxiliaries (40,000 troops) landed at Richborough before Claudius entered Camulodunum with war elephants.

narrative_blocks.title: Britain's Riches & Claudius's Need for Glory
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] Nearly ninety years after Julius Caesar sailed away, a nervous new ruler named **Emperor Claudius** took power in Rome in **AD 41**. Powerful **Roman senators** doubted Claudius because he walked with a **limp**, spoke with a **stutter**, and had never led an army. Claudius desperately needed a spectacular military triumph to win respect.

[2.2] Conquering misty island Britain promised both **military glory** and dazzling wealth. Rome wanted Britain's underground mines of **silver**, **Cornish tin**, **lead**, and **iron** to make coins, water pipes, and weapons. Fertile southern farms also grew abundant **wheat** to feed soldiers, while conquered tribes would have to pay heavy Roman **taxes**.

narrative_blocks.title: The Unstoppable Roman War Machine
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.3] Unlike Celtic farmers who fought part-time, Roman **legionaries** were full-time professional soldiers. Wearing hobnailed leather sandals called **caligae**, they marched **20 miles a day** carrying heavy packs and flexible iron strip armour called **lorica segmentata**. When arrows rained down, soldiers locked their curved rectangular **scutum** shields overhead and in front like a giant **testudo** ("tortoise") shell.

[2.4] Every legionary trained daily with deadly teamwork. First, soldiers hurled a heavy iron-tipped javelin called a **pilum**, cleverly designed to bend on impact so enemies could not throw it back. Then they stepped close behind their shield wall, using a short stabbing sword called a **gladius** with calm, unstoppable discipline.

narrative_blocks.title: Landing at Richborough & Elephants at Camulodunum
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.5] In **AD 43**, General **Aulus Plautius** sailed across the Channel with **four legions** and auxiliary troops — around **40,000 soldiers** in total. Landing at **Richborough** in Kent, the Romans built strong defensive ditches and marched inland. After a fierce two-day battle at the **River Medway**, they defeated the brave Celtic leader **Caratacus**.

[2.6] Plautius halted near the River Thames and sent word to Rome. **Emperor Claudius** arrived in person bringing towering **war elephants** that terrified Celtic horses with their strange smell and trumpeting roars. Claudius marched triumphantly into the tribal capital **Camulodunum** (**Colchester**), winning eleven kings' surrender and turning southern Britain into a Roman province.

sources.title: Source D: Richborough Roman Fort (Kent) & Cassius Dio's Account of AD 43
sources.caption: Massive Roman stone walls at Richborough (Rutupiae) in Kent — marking the historic landing beachhead of AD 43 — paired with Roman historian Cassius Dio's account.
sources.author: Roman Army Builders & Senator Cassius Dio (tr. Earnest Cary, 1925)
sources.context: Richborough guarded the Kent coast where General Aulus Plautius landed his 40,000 troops in AD 43. Notice in Cassius Dio's history that Roman soldiers were frightened at first to sail "outside the limits of the known world", before Claudius arrived with elephants! **Hinge Question:** Why did General Aulus Plautius pause near the River Thames and wait for Emperor Claudius to arrive in person before capturing Camulodunum?

sources.question: Read Cassius Dio's account alongside Source D. How did Roman soldiers feel before sailing, and how did Emperor Claudius make sure he got the credit for victory?

sources.text: Cassius Dio, Roman History, Book 60, Chapters 19–21: "Aulus Plautius, a senator of great renown, made a campaign against Britain [...] the soldiers were indignantly complaining at the thought of carrying on a campaign outside the limits of the known world. [...] When at last he did find them, he first defeated Caratacus and then Togodumnus [...] Claudius himself now joined the expedition, for which great preparations had been made, including even elephants; and taking charge of the legions that were waiting for him near the Thames, he crossed the stream, engaged the barbarians who had gathered at his approach, defeated them, and captured Camulodunum."

tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source B and Source C, a Roman legionary's kit helped him survive and win battles because every piece was designed for protection and teamwork. His lorica segmentata had overlapping iron strips on leather straps so sword blows bounced off while he could still march 20 miles a day. tasks.question: Explain TWO big reasons why Emperor Claudius decided to invade Britain in AD 43: one personal reason for Claudius himself, and one reason about Britain's riches.

tasks.model_answer: Emperor Claudius invaded Britain in AD 43 for two big reasons. First, Claudius personally needed military glory because powerful Roman senators mocked his limp and stutter and doubted a ruler who had never led soldiers. Second, Rome wanted Britain's rich natural resources, including silver for coins, lead for water pipes, Cornish tin, iron, golden wheat to feed the army, and new taxes from conquered tribes. That is why General Aulus Plautius waited by the Thames so Claudius could arrive in person with war elephants and claim the triumph at Camulodunum!

Even after our leader Caratacus fought bravely for two days at the River Medway, General Plautius's gleaming rows of iron lorica segmentata and red scutum shields kept coming! Suddenly, monstrous grey beasts taller than a roundhouse lumber through the mist — trumpeting war elephants brought by Emperor Claudius himself! Our chariot horses rear up in terror at their strange smell, and eleven tribal kings realise we cannot stop Rome's war machine today.

tasks.question: Big Question: Why did Emperor Claudius's invasion of AD 43 succeed in turning southern Britain into a Roman province when Julius Caesar had sailed away ninety-seven years earlier?
tasks.starter: Emperor Claudius succeeded in conquering southern Britain in AD 43 because Rome arrived prepared with...
hints: Show the massive scale of the AD 43 invasion under General Aulus Plautius (four legions — 40,000 soldiers landing at Richborough).

tasks.model_answer: Emperor Claudius succeeded in conquering southern Britain in AD 43 because Rome arrived prepared to stay rather than just raid and leave. General Aulus Plautius landed a huge force of 40,000 full-time troops at Richborough in Kent and built strong supply ditches right away. On the battlefield at the River Medway, disciplined legionaries wearing lorica segmentata used bending pilum javelins, short gladius swords, and locked testudo shields to defeat Caratacus's part-time tribal warriors. Finally, Claudius arrived with terrifying war elephants to capture Camulodunum, winning eleven kings' surrender and turning southern Britain into a permanent Roman province.

lessons.enquiryQuestion: Why did Queen Boudicca lead a huge rebellion against Rome in AD 60, and why did it fail?
lessons.enquiry_question: Why did Queen Boudicca lead a huge rebellion against Rome in AD 60, and why did it fail?
lessons.prologue: Seventeen years after Claudius's invasion, Roman Britain nearly collapsed in flames! Enraged by broken Roman promises and cruel treatment, Queen Boudicca of the Iceni united rebel tribes and burned three Roman towns into red ash — before facing 10,000 Roman legionaries in a narrow valley along Watling Street.
lessons.blurb: Seventeen years after Claudius's invasion, Roman Britain nearly collapsed in flames! Enraged by broken Roman promises and cruel treatment, Queen Boudicca of the Iceni united rebel tribes and burned three Roman towns into red ash — before facing 10,000 Roman legionaries in a narrow valley along Watling Street.

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry examines the most dramatic uprising in Roman Britain: Boudicca's Rebellion of AD 60–61. Pupils investigate why King Prasutagus's peaceful will to Emperor Nero was betrayed by greedy Roman officials, provoking Queen Boudicca of the Iceni and the neighbouring Trinovantes to rise up while Governor Suetonius Paulinus was campaigning far away in Anglesey. Pupils connect written accounts (Tacitus) with physical archaeology (the scorching red clay "destruction layer" beneath Colchester, London, and St Albans) before analysing why 10,000 disciplined legionaries defeated Boudicca's huge army in a narrow wooded valley at the Battle of Watling Street.

objectives.objective: Explain why broken Roman promises after King Prasutagus's death caused Queen Boudicca and the Iceni to rebel in AD 60.
objectives.primer: Unpack Prasutagus's will to Emperor Nero, stolen lands, sudden loan demands, and the flogging of Boudicca.
objectives.question: Why did Rome's treatment of a friendly ally like the Iceni turn peaceful tribes into fierce rebels?

objectives.objective: Describe how Boudicca burned Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium, and how the "red clay destruction layer" proves it.
objectives.primer: Use the map (Anglesey vs East Anglia) and explain how archaeologists find burnt red clay, ash, and melted pottery under London.
objectives.question: How do archaeologists digging beneath modern London know how fiercely Boudicca's fires burned?

objectives.objective: Analyse why Suetonius Paulinus's 10,000 legionaries defeated Boudicca's much larger army at the Battle of Watling Street.
objectives.primer: Focus on terrain (narrow wooded valley), tight Roman wedges, squashed Celtic swords, and the ring of family wagons behind.
objectives.question: Why did a narrow wooded valley and parked family wagons turn Boudicca's huge numbers into a trap?

source_context.Source A: Boudicca left no written diary of her own. Everything we read about her speeches and treatment comes from Roman writers — especially Tacitus, whose own father-in-law Agricola served as a young Roman officer in Britain during the revolt! **Hinge Question:** Why is it surprising that a Roman senator like Tacitus admitted Roman officers acted greedily and unfairly towards King Prasutagus's family?
source_context.Source B: When Boudicca attacked Camulodunum in AD 60, the proud Roman town had no strong stone city wall yet, so defenders were trapped inside the Temple of Claudius. Afterwards, Rome surrounded Colchester with thick stone walls and the giant Balkerne Gate! **Hinge Question:** What does building massive stone gates like the Balkerne Gate AFTER AD 61 tell us about how badly Boudicca shocked the Romans?
source_context.Source C: Studying the map explains WHY Boudicca succeeded at first! Governor Suetonius Paulinus and his main legions were hundreds of miles northwest attacking Druids on Anglesey, leaving south-east Britain's towns wide open. **Hinge Question:** Looking at Source C, how did the straight Roman road of Watling Street help Governor Suetonius Paulinus respond to the crisis?
source_context.Source D: Deep underneath modern London streets near this wall lies the "Boudiccan destruction layer" — a 40cm band of bright red burnt clay, ash, charred wheat, and melted bronze coins from AD 60. Above it, Rome rebuilt Londinium stronger than ever inside stone walls. **Hinge Question:** How do underground layers of burnt red clay AND surviving stone walls at Tower Hill work together to prove Tacitus's story is true?

narrative_blocks.title: Broken Roman Promises to the Iceni
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] At first, Rome let some friendly British rulers keep their thrones in peace. In **East Anglia**, **King Prasutagus** of the **Iceni** tribe stayed an ally of Rome. When Prasutagus died in **AD 60**, he left half his wealth to **Emperor Nero** and half to his two daughters, trusting Rome to protect his family.

[3.2] Greedy Roman officials cruelly broke that promise. Soldiers marched into Iceni lands, seized noble families' farms, and demanded that heavy Roman **loans** and taxes be paid back at once. When **Queen Boudicca** protested against this injustice, Roman officers had her **flogged** with whips and **mistreated her daughters**, sparking fury across East Anglia.

narrative_blocks.title: Three Roman Towns Burn to Red Clay
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.3] Riding tall in her wooden war chariot, **Queen Boudicca** united the **Iceni**, the neighbouring **Trinovantes**, and other angry tribes. Better still for the rebels, Roman Governor **Suetonius Paulinus** was marching hundreds of miles away in **Anglesey** in north Wales. Boudicca struck first at **Camulodunum** (**Colchester**), burning the hated Roman temple to ashes.

[3.4] Next, Boudicca's huge rebel army swept south and torched the bustling port of **Londinium** (**London**) before destroying **Verulamium** (**St Albans**). Timber shops and clay-walled houses burned so fiercely that they baked into a scorching **red clay "destruction layer"**. Even today, **archaeologists** digging deep beneath modern London streets still uncover blackened coins and melted pottery!

narrative_blocks.title: Showdown at the Battle of Watling Street (AD 61)
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.5] In **AD 61**, Governor **Suetonius Paulinus** raced back along the Roman road called **Watling Street** with **10,000 disciplined legionaries**. Although heavily outnumbered, Suetonius cleverly chose a **narrow wooded valley** that protected his sides. Confident of victory, Iceni families parked a half-circle of **wooden wagons** behind the battlefield to watch.

[3.6] When the Britons charged, the narrow funnel squashed Boudicca's warriors together so they could barely swing their long swords. Advancing in **tight wedges**, Roman soldiers hurled javelins and pushed the rebels backward until they were trapped against their own **ring of wagons**. Rome won, Boudicca died soon after, and **Londinium** was rebuilt inside mighty **stone walls**.

tasks.model_answer: Historians piece together Boudicca's rebellion using both written words and archaeology. First, Tacitus in Source A explains why the revolt started: King Prasutagus left half his kingdom to Emperor Nero in peace, yet Roman officials plundered Iceni homes and mistreated Boudicca's family. Second, archaeologists digging deep beneath modern London, Colchester, and St Albans uncover a scorching red clay destruction layer full of blackened coins and melted pottery, proving those three towns really burned in AD 60! Even though we read Tacitus carefully because only Romans wrote accounts down, the burnt soil beneath our feet backs up his story.

tasks.question: Boudicca had a much bigger army than Governor Suetonius Paulinus! Explain why her rebellion still failed at the Battle of Watling Street in AD 61.
tasks.starter: Even though Boudicca had far more warriors, her army lost the Battle of Watling Street because...
hints: Explain how Suetonius Paulinus cleverly used the landscape by choosing a narrow wooded valley that protected his sides.
Describe what happened when the Britons charged into the narrow funnel (squashed long swords vs tight Roman wedges).

tasks.model_answer: Even though Boudicca had far more warriors, her army lost the Battle of Watling Street because Governor Suetonius Paulinus chose the battlefield brilliantly. He lined up his 10,000 disciplined legionaries inside a narrow wooded valley so the huge British crowd could not surround his sides. When the Britons charged into that tight funnel, they got squashed together so closely that warriors could barely swing their long slashing swords! Advancing calmly in tight wedges after hurling their javelins, the Romans pushed the rebels backward until they were trapped against their own parked ring of wooden family wagons.

tasks.model_answer: Queen Boudicca's rebellion in AD 60 was caused by cruel Roman greed when officials betrayed King Prasutagus's will to Emperor Nero, stole Iceni lands, demanded loans back, and flogged Boudicca. Taking advantage of Governor Suetonius campaigning far away in Anglesey, Boudicca united angry tribes and burned Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium into a red clay destruction layer. Although 10,000 Roman legionaries won the Battle of Watling Street in AD 61 using a narrow wooded valley and tight wedges, Rome learned a big lesson — rebuilding Colchester and Londinium inside mighty stone walls and treating friendly British leaders more fairly.

lessons.enquiryQuestion: Why did Emperor Hadrian build a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain, and who guarded it?
lessons.enquiry_question: Why did Emperor Hadrian build a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain, and who guarded it?
lessons.prologue: In AD 122, Emperor Hadrian ordered Roman soldiers to build a 73-mile stone wall right across northern Britain from sea to sea. Buried in wet mud and carved onto stone tombstones, amazing clues reveal birthday parties, woollen socks, and soldiers from Europe, Syria, and North Africa guarding the cold frontier!
lessons.blurb: In AD 122, Emperor Hadrian ordered Roman soldiers to build a 73-mile stone wall right across northern Britain from sea to sea. Buried in wet mud and carved onto stone tombstones, amazing clues reveal birthday parties, woollen socks, and soldiers from Europe, Syria, and North Africa guarding the cold frontier!

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry takes pupils to Rome's north-west frontier from AD 122 onwards. Pupils discover why Emperor Hadrian constructed a 73-mile (80 Roman mile) stone barrier between the River Tyne and the Solway Firth — not as an impenetrable seal, but as a controlled customs and military zone punctuated by milecastles, turrets, and 16 garrison forts like Housesteads. Using the anaerobic Vindolanda ink tablets (Tab. Vindol. II 291 & 346) and epigraphic tombstones at Burgh-by-Sands and Arbeia (RIB 1064 & 1065), pupils uncover both intimate domestic life and the remarkable multi-continental diversity of Roman Britain's frontier communities.

objectives.objective: Explain why Emperor Hadrian ordered a 73-mile wall across northern Britain in AD 122 and how milecastles and forts worked.
objectives.primer: Clarify that milecastles had gates both north and south to regulate movement, prevent raids from Caledonia, and tax cross-border trade.
objectives.question: How did milecastles and forts like Housesteads let Rome control movement across the frontier?

objectives.objective: Use the Vindolanda wooden ink tablets as primary evidence for everyday life on the northern frontier.
objectives.primer: Examine how oxygen-free mud preserved Claudia Severa's birthday invitation (Tab. Vindol. II 291) and a soldier's parcel of woollen socks and underpants (II 346).
objectives.question: What do the Vindolanda letters reveal that stone fort walls alone could never tell us?

objectives.objective: Investigate archaeological and tombstone evidence showing soldiers and civilians from Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa living along the Wall.
objectives.primer: Highlight Batavians, Syrian archers, Aurelian Moors at Burgh-by-Sands, and Barates, Regina, and Victor at Arbeia Fort.
objectives.question: How do inscriptions at Arbeia and Burgh-by-Sands prove that Roman Britain's frontier was home to people from three continents?

source_context.Source A: Every single Roman mile along the 73-mile frontier, soldiers built a fortified stone gatehouse called a milecastle where patrols checked travellers, stopped cattle raids, and collected customs taxes. **Hinge Question:** Why did Emperor Hadrian include guarded gateways every mile along his Wall instead of blocking off the north completely?
source_context.Source B: Housesteads was one of 16 major stone forts backing Hadrian's Wall, housing around 800 soldiers. Keeping hundreds of troops healthy required stone drains, water tanks, and communal flushing toilets. **Hinge Question:** Why did Roman army commanders spend so much time building clean stone toilets and drains at remote frontier forts?
source_context.Source C: Preserved for nearly 2,000 years in wet, oxygen-free mud at Vindolanda just south of Hadrian's Wall, wooden ink letters reveal warm friendships, family life, and parcels of socks and underpants sent to chilly soldiers. **Hinge Question:** How do personal wooden letters like Claudia Severa's invitation change our view of life at a Roman frontier fort?
source_context.Source D: Arbeia guarded sea supplies for Hadrian's Wall. Tombstones found outside the fort prove that people from Syria, North Africa (Mauretania), Spain, and southern British tribes lived side by side along the Tyne. **Hinge Question:** Why are carved Roman tombstones at forts like Arbeia such valuable clues for historians studying who lived in Roman Britain?

items.question: What cone-roofed homes made of wattle-and-daub and thatch did Iron Age Britons live in before the Romans arrived?
items.explanation: Iron Age families cooked, slept, and wove wool around a central fire inside circular thatched roundhouses.

items.question: Why did Julius Caesar sail to Britain twice in 55 BC and 54 BC without staying permanently?
items.answer: He won battles and tribute promises, then returned to Gaul rather than conquering the island
items.explanation: Caesar raided south-east Britain in 55 BC and 54 BC, leaving full conquest until nearly a century later.

items.question: Which Roman Emperor launched the permanent invasion of Britain in AD 43 with four legions and war elephants?
items.explanation: In AD 43, Emperor Claudius sent General Aulus Plautius with 40,000 troops and arrived with elephants at Camulodunum (Colchester).

items.question: What was the tortoise-like shield formation called when Roman legionaries locked rectangular shields overhead and in front?
items.explanation: Locking scutum shields together formed a protective shell against enemy spears, stones, and arrows.

items.question: Why did Roman soldiers become such tough, disciplined fighters compared with part-time tribal warriors?
items.answer: They were full-time professional soldiers who trained daily and marched up to 20 miles carrying heavy kit
items.explanation: Legionaries served for 25 years, wearing iron strip armour (lorica segmentata) and carrying throwing spears (pila) and short swords (gladii).

items.question: Which warrior queen of the Iceni tribe led a massive rebellion against Roman rule in AD 60–61?
items.explanation: After Romans seized Iceni lands and mistreated her daughters following King Prasutagus's death, Boudicca led a huge uprising.

items.question: Name the three Roman towns burned to the ground by Boudicca's rebel army in AD 60–61.
items.explanation: Archaeologists still find a dark red layer of burnt clay and ash beneath Colchester, London, and St Albans from Boudicca's revolt.

items.question: Along which Roman road line did Governor Suetonius Paulinus defeat Boudicca's much larger army using narrow ground and discipline?
items.explanation: Choosing a narrow funnel backed by woods, 10,000 disciplined Roman troops held firm with shield walls and javelins against Boudicca's host.

current_items.question: In what year did Emperor Hadrian visit Britain and order a stone wall across the north?
current_items.explanation: Emperor Hadrian inspected Britain in AD 122 and ordered his legions to build a sea-to-sea frontier wall.

current_items.question: How many modern miles long was Hadrian's Wall from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway?
current_items.explanation: Hadrian's Wall ran for 80 Roman miles — about 73 modern miles — from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth.

current_items.question: What natural condition preserved wooden ink letters underground at Vindolanda Fort?
current_items.explanation: Waterlogged, oxygen-free soil stopped bacteria from rotting the wafer-thin wooden tablets.

current_items.question: Who wrote the famous AD 100 birthday party invitation found at Vindolanda?
current_items.explanation: Claudia Severa's greeting to Sulpicia Lepidina contains the oldest known Latin handwriting by a woman.

current_items.question: From which three continents did auxiliary troops come to guard Hadrian's Wall?
current_items.answer: Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa
current_items.explanation: Regiments included European Batavians, Syrian archers from the Middle East, and Aurelian Moors from North Africa.

narrative_blocks.title: 73 Miles of Stone From Sea to Sea (AD 122)
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] In **AD 122**, **Emperor Hadrian** visited Britain and ordered his legions to build a mighty stone **frontier** wall across the north. Stretching **73 miles** (**80 Roman miles**) from **Wallsend** on the River Tyne to **Bowness-on-Solway**, **Hadrian's Wall** separated Roman Britain from **Caledonia** (modern Scotland) and showed Rome's power from sea to sea.

[4.2] At every Roman mile, soldiers built a guarded gatehouse called a **milecastle** to stop surprise cattle raids and collect **taxes** from peaceful traders crossing the border. Two stone watchtowers stood between each milecastle, backed by **16 large forts** such as **Housesteads**, where flowing rainwater channels flushed communal multi-seat stone **latrines**.

narrative_blocks.title: Postcards in the Mud: The Vindolanda Tablets
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.3] Just south of the Wall stood **Vindolanda Fort**, where deep, wet, **oxygen-free mud** stopped buried wood and leather from rotting away. Archaeologists dug up hundreds of wafer-thin **wooden ink tablets** **preserved** underground since around **AD 100**, capturing real family voices from the chilly northern frontier.

[4.4] On one famous tablet, a fort commander's wife named **Claudia Severa** warmly invited her dearest friend **Sulpicia Lepidina** to her **birthday party** on 11 September — the oldest surviving **Latin handwriting by a woman**! Another tablet lists a parcel sent to keep a cold soldier cosy: warm **woollen socks**, two pairs of **sandals**, and two pairs of **underpants**.

narrative_blocks.title: Soldiers & Families From Across the Roman Empire
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.5] Hadrian's Wall was guarded by **auxiliary** regiments recruited from **three continents** — Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. **Batavian** troops from the Netherlands served at Vindolanda, **Syrian archers** watched the hills from Carvoran, and North African **Aurelian Moors** stood guard near the western coast at **Burgh-by-Sands**.

[4.6] Bustling civilian settlements called **vici** grew outside the fort gates where soldiers' families, craftspeople, and traders lived together. At **Arbeia Fort** (South Shields), a Syrian flag-trader named **Barates** married **Regina**, a freedwoman from the British **Catuvellauni** tribe, while another carved tombstone honours **Victor**, a young freedman from **Mauretania** in North Africa.

tasks.model_answer: Looking at Source C, the Vindolanda wooden tablets give us amazing clues about real life on the frontier because they show ordinary families and friendships, not just battles. Another tablet lists warm woollen socks, sandals, and underpants sent to a chilly soldier, proving how cold northern Britain felt while showing human details that stone walls alone could never reveal.

tasks.question: Why did Emperor Hadrian order a 73-mile stone wall with milecastle gates and 16 forts across northern Britain in AD 122?
tasks.starter: Emperor Hadrian ordered his legions to build a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain in AD 122 because...
hints: Describe where the Wall ran (73 miles from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway) separating Roman Britain from Caledonia.
Explain the two main jobs of the guarded milecastle gates: stopping northern raids and collecting taxes from traders.
Scholar Challenge (Year 5+): Explain why having gates every Roman mile proves the Wall was designed as a controlled border checkpoint rather than a sealed barrier.
tasks.model_answer: Emperor Hadrian ordered his legions to build a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain in AD 122 because he wanted to protect Roman Britain from raids out of Caledonia and control everyone crossing the border. Stretching from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway, the Wall had a guarded milecastle gate every Roman mile, two watchtowers in between, and 16 forts like Housesteads behind it. Rather than blocking people completely, milecastle gates let peaceful farmers and merchants pass through once soldiers checked their goods and collected Roman taxes.

tasks.model_answer: Pulling my woollen cloak tight against the icy Northumberland wind on Hadrian's Wall, my life far from my warm North African homeland is tough but proud. As an auxiliary soldier, I check farmers' carts and collect taxes at our milecastle gate while scanning the misty hills of Caledonia for raiders. Off duty inside the stone fort, rainwater flushes our communal latrines, and I am grateful for my thick woollen socks! Outside the fort gates in the bustling vicus town, I hear Latin, Celtic, and Syrian voices mingling as families from three continents share life on the edge of the Empire.

tasks.question: Big Question: What do Vindolanda's letters and Arbeia's tombstones prove about the diversity of people living along Rome's northern frontier?
tasks.starter: Archaeological clues from Vindolanda and Arbeia prove that Rome's northern frontier was home to a remarkably diverse community because...
hints: Name auxiliary troops from across the Empire: European Batavians, Syrian archers, and North African Aurelian Moors at Burgh-by-Sands.

tasks.model_answer: Archaeological clues from Vindolanda and Arbeia prove that Rome's northern frontier was home to a remarkably diverse community drawn from three continents — Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. Auxiliary regiments included Batavians from the Netherlands, Syrian archers, and North African Aurelian Moors at Burgh-by-Sands. Outside the forts in busy vici towns, families and merchants settled too: Vindolanda's wooden letters reveal commanders' wives like Claudia Severa, while carved tombstones at Arbeia honour Barates from Syria, his British wife Regina from the Catuvellauni tribe, and Victor, a freedman from Mauretania in North Africa.

lessons.prologue: Roman engineers laid 10,000 miles of straight stone roads, piped fresh water into steaming bathhouses like Aquae Sulis, and heated dolphin-mosaic villas from underneath! Yet out in the countryside, did life really change for everyone?

teacher_notes.primer: This Change & Continuity enquiry explores the urban and technological revolution of Roman Britain alongside deep rural continuity. Pupils examine groma-surveyed cambered stone highways, planned towns with forums, basilicas, and amphitheatres (Caerleon), aqueduct water engineering, Aquae Sulis bathhouses, and hypocaust pilae heating. Crucially, Act 3 balances elite villas like Fishbourne Palace and imported Mediterranean foods (grapes, cherries, walnuts, garum) against archaeological reality: roughly 90% of Britons remained rural farmers living in thatched roundhouses while paying Roman taxes.

source_context.Source A: Using a wooden sighting instrument called a groma, Roman engineers laid 10,000 miles of layered stone roads across Britain with cambered surfaces and side ditches so rainwater ran straight off. **Hinge Question:** Why was building 10,000 miles of all-weather stone roads essential for keeping Roman control over Britain?
source_context.Source B: Major Roman towns and fortress settlements featured oval stone amphitheatres where up to 6,000 soldiers and townspeople cheered gladiator bouts, beast hunts, and military parades. **Hinge Question:** Why did Roman governors and wealthy town leaders pay for free gladiator shows inside grand stone amphitheatres?
source_context.Source C: Both public bathhouses like Aquae Sulis (Bath) and wealthy countryside villas used hypocaust central heating: enslaved stokers kept a furnace burning so hot air circulated between stacks of brick tiles (pilae) under mosaic floors. **Hinge Question:** Who did the hard, smoky work needed to keep luxurious Roman bathhouses and villa floors warm?
source_context.Source D: Wealthy Romano-British elites — such as allied British rulers and senior officials — decorated grand stone villas like Fishbourne with colourful mosaic floors while almost nine out of ten rural Britons kept living in thatched roundhouses. **Hinge Question:** Does a magnificent mosaic floor at Fishbourne Palace prove that EVERY family in Roman Britain lived in luxury?

items.explanation: Boudicca burned Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium before being defeated at Watling Street.

items.question: In what year did Emperor Hadrian order a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain?
items.explanation: Begun in AD 122, Hadrian's Wall stretched 73 miles from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway.

items.question: What were the fortified stone gatehouses placed at every Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall called?
items.explanation: Soldiers stationed at milecastles stopped northern raids and collected border taxes from traders.

items.question: What preserved Claudia Severa's birthday invitation and the woollen socks letter at Vindolanda Fort?
items.explanation: Waterlogged, oxygen-free mud prevented the thin wooden ink tablets from rotting away.

items.question: What do the tombstones of Barates, Regina, and Victor at Arbeia Fort prove about Roman Britain?
items.answer: People from Syria, North Africa, and British tribes lived side by side on the frontier

current_items.question: What sighting tool did Roman surveyors use to build 10,000 miles of straight stone roads?
current_items.explanation: Surveyors lined up hanging plumb-weights on a wooden groma cross to plot dead-straight highways.

current_items.question: What was the central open marketplace at the heart of every Roman town called?
current_items.explanation: Townspeople met in the forum to shop, trade, hear announcements, and visit the basilica town hall.

current_items.question: What Roman name was given to the famous spring-fed bathhouse town of modern Bath?
current_items.explanation: Aquae Sulis combined Roman engineering with sacred hot springs dedicated to the goddess Sulis Minerva.

current_items.question: What did Romans call their underfloor central heating system supported by brick pilae stacks?
current_items.explanation: Hot air from a wood furnace circulated beneath floors raised on brick pilae pillars.

current_items.question: Roughly how many Britons out of ten carried on farming in countryside roundhouses during Roman rule?
current_items.answer: Almost nine out of ten Britons

narrative_blocks.title: Straight Stone Roads & Bustling Market Forums
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] Before Rome arrived, Britons travelled slowly along muddy dirt tracks. Roman surveyors used a wooden sighting tool called a **groma** to lay **10,000 miles** of dead-straight stone highways across Britain. Soldiers stacked rammed gravel and **cambered** (gently curved) paving stones between deep **side ditches** so rainwater drained quickly away and heavy carts moved in all weathers.

[5.2] Where major highways met, Romans built planned grid towns protected by tall stone walls. At each town's heart stood the **forum** — a bustling open marketplace edged by busy shops and a grand town hall called a **basilica** — while oval stone **amphitheatres** like **Caerleon** in South Wales seated thousands of cheering spectators for **gladiator** shows.

narrative_blocks.title: Aqueducts, Steam Baths & Underfloor Heating
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] Stone water channels called **aqueducts** and underground **lead pipes** carried fresh spring water straight into Roman towns to feed street fountains, flushing sewers, and public bathhouses like **Aquae Sulis** (modern **Bath**). Visiting the noisy baths was a favourite daily routine where townspeople went to exercise, chat with friends, and wash clean.

[5.4] Bathhouses and rich homes used **hypocaust** underfloor central heating. Enslaved workers stoked a roaring wood furnace so hot air blew beneath floors raised on neat brick tile stacks called **pilae**. Bathers relaxed in warm and steaming hot rooms before scraping perfumed **olive oil**, sweat, and dirt from their skin with a curved bronze **strigil**.

narrative_blocks.title: Dolphin Mosaics vs Countryside Roundhouses
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] In peaceful southern Britain, wealthy Roman officials and friendly Celtic tribal leaders built grand stone country **villas** like **Fishbourne Palace** in Sussex. Skilled craftspeople pressed thousands of tiny coloured stone cubes called **tesserae** into wet mortar to create **mosaic** floors, while diners feasted on new Roman foods including **grapes**, **cherries**, **walnuts**, and salty fish sauce called **garum**.

[5.6] Yet Roman rule did not change everyone's home equally across the island. Out in the countryside, almost **nine out of ten Britons** carried on farming the land inside smoky **thatched roundhouses**, speaking Celtic languages while working hard to pay **Roman taxes**.

tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Sources C and D, we can tell that wealthy villa owners lived in great comfort because their stone homes had both central heating and dazzling artwork. tasks.model_answer: Roman engineers transformed travel and town hygiene across Britain by building 10,000 miles of stone highways and clever water networks. tasks.model_answer: Walking along the straight, cambered stone road through the town gate, my afternoon in a Roman town begins in the noisy central forum! Stalls beside the grand basilica sell sweet cherries, walnuts, and jars of salty garum fish sauce, while crowds cheer gladiator practice at the oval stone amphitheatre nearby. Next, I head to the public bathhouse fed by stone aqueducts. Inside the steaming hot room, the mosaic floor feels toastily warm above its brick hypocaust pillars as I chat with friends and scrape olive oil from my skin with a curved bronze strigil — so different from my cousins farming in their smoky thatched roundhouse!

tasks.question: Big Question: Did Roman roads, bathhouses, and stone villas change everyday life for EVERYONE in Britain? Weigh up both change and continuity!
tasks.starter: Roman rule brought dramatic changes to Britain's towns and wealthy homes, yet everyday life did not change equally for everyone because...
hints: Describe the big changes in towns and rich villas: 10,000 miles of stone roads, forums, Aquae Sulis baths, hypocaust heating, mosaics, and new foods.

tasks.model_answer: Roman rule brought dramatic changes to Britain's towns and wealthy homes, yet everyday life did not change equally for everyone. For town-dwellers and rich tribal leaders in villas like Fishbourne Palace, life was transformed by 10,000 miles of stone roads, bustling forums, aqueduct water, steaming bathhouses like Aquae Sulis, hypocaust heating, dolphin mosaics, and foods like cherries and garum. However, almost nine out of ten ordinary Britons carried on farming in the countryside inside thatched timber roundhouses and speaking Celtic languages — though even they had to grow extra grain to pay Roman taxes!

source_context.Source A: By AD 410, Visigoth armies were attacking Italy itself while Picts, Scotti, Angles, and Saxons raided Britain. With no spare legions left, Emperor Honorius wrote telling British cities to defend themselves. **Hinge Question:** Did the Romans leave Britain in AD 410 because Britain defeated them, or because Rome itself was in terrible danger?
source_context.Source B: Packed neatly inside a wooden chest with gold bracelets, silver spoons, and over 15,000 coins, the Hoxne Hoard was buried after AD 407 and only rediscovered in 1992 when a farmer searched a Suffolk field for a lost hammer! **Hinge Question:** What does the fact that nobody ever came back to dig up the Hoxne Hoard suggest about Britain around AD 410?
source_context.Source C: Discovered in Suffolk in 1942 alongside 33 other silver spoons, bowls, and platters, the Great Dish of the Mildenhall Treasure shows both dazzling 4th-century wealth and the sudden fear that drove families to bury silver hoards. **Hinge Question:** Why did so many buried silver hoards turn up in eastern Britain near the North Sea coast?
source_context.Source D: Built with neat courses of small limestone blocks and red tile bands around AD 306, York's Multangular Tower is a visible reminder that Britain's major cities, roads, language, and calendar still stand on Roman foundations today. **Hinge Question:** Which Roman legacy affects your own life more every day: surviving stone towers like Source D, or invisible legacies like our ABC alphabet and calendar?

narrative_blocks.title: Raiders on Every Coast & Leaving in AD 410
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.1] After nearly four centuries of rule, the mighty **Roman Empire** came under fierce attack everywhere at once. Around **AD 400**, **Picts** from Scotland, **Scotti** from Ireland, and seafaring **Angles and Saxons** from across the North Sea raided Britain's coasts and villages, while **Visigoth** armies invaded **Italy** and threatened **Rome** itself.

[6.2] One by one, Roman legions marched away from Britain and sailed across the Channel to defend the heart of the Empire. When worried British leaders wrote begging for military help in **AD 410**, **Emperor Honorius** sent a famous reply warning that Rome had no spare soldiers left and **British towns must defend themselves**.

narrative_blocks.title: Buried Silver Treasure & Crumbling Bathhouses
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.3] Once the Roman army left, fresh shipments of **Roman coins** stopped arriving to pay soldiers' wages. Busy town markets shrank, potters' workshops closed down, and nobody repaired leaky stone aqueducts, **hypocausts**, or public bathhouses, which slowly crumbled into silent, overgrown ruins.

[6.4] Fearing coastal raiders and dangerous times, anxious wealthy families packed chests of gold coins, silver spoons, pepper pots, and heavy banquet plates underground as a secret **hoard**, hoping to dig them up when peace returned. Many owners never came back: centuries later, farmers ploughing fields in Suffolk unearthed glittering Roman treasures like the **Hoxne Hoard** and the **Mildenhall Treasure**.

narrative_blocks.title: Roman Footprints Still Shaping Britain Today
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.5] Even though the legions marched away, Rome's lasting **legacy** still shapes Britain all around us today. Bustling **Londinium** grew into our capital city **London**, towns ending in **-chester** or **-caster** — like Manchester and Lancaster — mark old Roman forts (**castra**), and modern **A-roads** still follow dead-straight Roman highways.

[6.6] Every single day we write using the **Latin** **ABC alphabet**, read **Roman numerals** (**I, V, X**) on clockfaces, and track the year with the **12-month calendar** naming **July** (Julius Caesar) and **August** (Emperor Augustus) after Roman leaders. Rome even brought **Christianity**, written laws, sweet **apples**, **cabbages**, **rabbits**, and **stinging nettles** to Britain!

Without Roman soldiers to guard villas and towns, rich families packed silver pepper pots, spoons, heavy banquet dishes, and thousands of coins into chests as a secret hoard, planning to dig them up when peace returned. The fact that nobody ever came back — leaving Suffolk farmers to find them over 1,500 years later — proves how suddenly safety collapsed around AD 410.

Scholar Challenge (Year 5+): Trace the knock-on effect of soldiers leaving: why did stopping army wages make town markets shrink and bathhouses crumble?
tasks.model_answer: The Roman army marched away from Britain around AD 410 because the Roman Empire was under attack everywhere at once. While Picts from Scotland, Scotti from Ireland, and Angles and Saxons across the North Sea raided Britain, Visigoth armies invaded Italy and threatened Rome itself. Legions were called back to save Italy, and in AD 410 Emperor Honorius told British towns they must defend themselves. Without soldiers' wages arriving, new Roman coins disappeared, town workshops shut down, and leaky aqueducts, hypocausts, and stone bathhouses slowly crumbled into ruins.

Terrible news reached our town forum that Emperor Honorius cannot send soldiers and we must defend ourselves against Angles and Saxons raiding from the North Sea. Back at our villa, the hypocaust furnace stands cold and markets have run out of new coins. Carefully, we wrap our silver spoons, banquet dish, and coins inside an oak chest as a secret hoard, stamping soil flat over the pit and praying we will return when safe days come back.

tasks.question: Big Question: Even though the Roman legions left in AD 410, what was Rome's greatest lasting legacy for Britain today?
tasks.starter: Even though the Roman legions marched away in AD 410, Rome changed Britain forever by leaving behind...
hints: Include towns and travel: Londinium becoming London, -chester/-caster fort towns (from castra), and modern A-roads along straight Roman routes.

Scholar Challenge (Year 5+): Choose which single Roman legacy you think matters MOST to your daily life today (such as our ABC alphabet, cities, laws, Christianity, or foods like apples and cabbages) and explain why!
tasks.model_answer: Even though the Roman legions marched away in AD 410, Rome changed Britain forever by leaving behind a legacy we still use every single day. On our maps, Londinium grew into our capital city London, towns ending in -chester or -caster mark Roman forts (castra), and modern A-roads still follow straight Roman highways. Even more importantly, Rome gave us the Latin ABC alphabet we read and write with, Roman numerals (I, V, X) on clocks, the 12-month calendar including July and August, written laws, Christianity, and everyday foods and wildlife from apples and cabbages to rabbits and stinging nettles!

key_individuals.name: Julius Caesar
key_individuals.role: Roman General Who Led the First Expeditions to Britain (55 & 54 BC)
key_individuals.origins: Ambitious Roman general who conquered Gaul (modern France) and looked across the English Channel towards southern Britain.
key_individuals.significance: Led two reconnaissance expeditions to Kent in 55 BC and 54 BC and wrote the earliest surviving eyewitness account of Iron Age British tribes and war chariots.
achievements: Landed Roman legionaries on the shingled beaches of Kent in 55 BC and returned with 800 ships in 54 BC.
Recorded valuable written descriptions of British chariot tactics, timber forts, and trade links in The Gallic War.
Returned to Gaul without leaving a permanent garrison—meaning Britain remained independent for another 97 years until AD 43.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Julius Caesar raided southern Britain twice (55 & 54 BC) and sailed back to Gaul; Emperor Claudius launched the permanent conquest nearly a century later in AD 43.

key_individuals.name: Emperor Claudius
key_individuals.role: Roman Emperor Who Conquered Southern Britain (Reigned AD 41–54)
key_individuals.origins: Became Emperor in AD 41 despite walking with a limp and speaking with a stutter; doubted by powerful Roman senators because he had never commanded an army.
key_individuals.significance: Ordered General Aulus Plautius and 40,000 Roman troops to invade Britain in spring AD 43, personally arriving with war elephants to capture Camulodunum (Colchester).
achievements: Dispatched four Roman legions and 20,000 auxiliary soldiers across the Channel to Richborough in Kent in AD 43.
Entered Camulodunum with war elephants and accepted the surrender of eleven British kings.
Turned southern Britain into the wealthy new Roman province of Britannia, rich in tin, silver, lead, iron, and grain.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Claudius spent just sixteen days in Britain, yet his AD 43 invasion began nearly 370 years of Roman rule.

key_individuals.name: Queen Boudicca
key_individuals.role: Queen of the Iceni & Leader of the Great Rebellion Against Rome
key_individuals.origins: Ruler of the Iceni tribe in East Anglia alongside her husband King Prasutagus, who had been a peaceful ally of Rome.
key_individuals.significance: United the Iceni and Trinovantes in AD 60 after Roman officials broke their treaty, seized Iceni lands, flogged Boudicca, and attacked her daughters.
achievements: Burned the Roman towns of Camulodunum (Colchester), Londinium (London), and Verulamium (St Albans), leaving a layer of red burnt clay still dug up today.
Led tens of thousands of British warriors against Roman Governor Suetonius Paulinus at the Battle of Watling Street.
Remembered nearly two millennia later as a powerful symbol of resistance against injustice, honoured by a bronze statue beside Westminster Bridge.
key_individuals.key_distinction: No Iceni writings survive—everything written about Boudicca comes from Roman historians Tacitus and Cassius Dio, backed up by burnt archaeological layers underground.

key_individuals.name: Emperor Hadrian
key_individuals.role: Roman Emperor Who Ordered the 73-Mile Northern Frontier Wall (AD 122)
key_individuals.origins: Widely travelled Roman Emperor who toured the frontiers of his vast empire in person rather than staying in Rome.
key_individuals.significance: Visited Britain in AD 122 and ordered Roman legionaries to build a 73-mile (80-Roman-mile) stone frontier wall from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth.
achievements: Designed a coast-to-coast frontier fortification with guarded Milecastle gates every Roman mile and sixteen major stone forts like Housesteads.
Controlled cross-border raids from Caledonia while collecting customs taxes on peaceful trade through Milecastle gates.
Created a UNESCO World Heritage monument whose stone crags, bathhouses, and barracks still stand across northern England today.

key_individuals.name: Claudia Severa
key_individuals.role: Fort Commander's Wife & Author of the Famous Vindolanda Birthday Invitation
key_individuals.origins: Roman noblewoman living on the chilly northern British frontier as the wife of fort commander Aelius Brocchus near Hadrian’s Wall.
key_individuals.significance: Sent a wooden ink letter (Vindolanda Tablet 291) warmly inviting her close friend Sulpicia Lepidina at Vindolanda to celebrate her birthday on 11 September.
achievements: Added a personal farewell message in her own hand ("Farewell, sister, my dearest soul"), preserved in wet oxygen-free mud for nearly 2,000 years.
Wrote the earliest surviving example of Latin handwriting by a woman anywhere in the Roman world.

key_individuals.name: Regina & Barates of Palmyra
key_individuals.role: Multicultural Couple Honoured at Arbeia Roman Fort (South Shields)
key_individuals.origins: Regina was born into the British Catuvellauni tribe in southern England; Barates travelled over 2,500 miles from Palmyra in Syria as a military flag-merchant.
key_individuals.significance: After freeing and marrying Regina, Barates commissioned an ornate stone memorial at Arbeia Fort near the eastern end of Hadrian’s Wall when she died aged thirty.
achievements: Carved Regina’s memorial in TWO languages—Latin across the main stone and Barates’s own Aramaic language underneath ("Regina, the freedwoman of Barates, alas!").
Provides vivid archaeological proof—alongside North African Aurelian Moors at Burgh-by-Sands—that Roman Britain connected people across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East.
